title: Ang 1157–1162: Kabir in Bhairao
tomorrow: what happens when a child begs God to drink his milk?

lines: COINS IN THE CORNER OF A CLOTH.
cards: Money now is mostly a number on a screen. You can't feel it in your hand or hear it clink. For a long time, in a lot of places, you kept it tied in a knot in the corner of a cloth: a scarf, a turban end, a dupatta.
You could feel it against you all day, a little hard lump that said you're safe. On ang 1157 the weaver Kabir picks up that knot and refuses to tie it.

teach.b: Here the Gurus' Bhairao hymns end and the Bhagats begin, the saint-poets whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth. First comes Kabir, remembered as a weaver.
In paraphrase, his hymn opens: this wealth of mine is the Lord's Name. I don't tie it in a knot. I don't sell it to buy my food.
Feel the two things he's turning down. The knot is guarding: wealth you clutch, check, worry about.
Selling is spending: wealth you trade away for something else. Ordinary money is always one or the other, saved or spent. Kabir says the Name, Naam, is neither.
You can't lock it up, and you can't cash it out. It isn't less real for that; the hymn calls it his wealth, his capital.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Granth puts a weaver's hymns right beside the Gurus' own, in the same raga, after the same morning hymns, as scripture.

Notice too what Kabir doesn't say. He doesn't say money is evil, or that you shouldn't save. He's talking about a different kind of wealth, the kind you can't feel against your hip, and saying it's the one he trusts.

how: Kabir's Bhairao hymns are sung in kirtan like the Gurus' own; Sikhs read the Bhagats' hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, bowing to the whole of it as the Guru.

o: where Ravidas closes Bhairao: what is seen will pass
where Kabir's Bhairao hymns begin: the Name as wealth
where Guru Arjan says he's neither Hindu nor Muslim

games.q: Kabir's two refusals — tap the pairs.
p: a weaver, the first Bhagat in Bhairao

s: Kabir is one of the Sikh Gurus
he's a Bhagat, a saint-poet whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth.
Kabir's hymn tells people never to save money
the wealth he won't knot up or sell is the Name; he isn't giving money advice.
Kabir's hymns sit in the Granth beside the Gurus' own, in the same raga
in Bhairao, they come right after the Gurus' hymns.

games.q: a friend gets their first paycheck and texts: "Kabir says don't tie wealth in a knot. so I shouldn't save?" what do you send back?
o: his line is about the Name, a wealth you can't store or sell. saving a paycheck is a different question.
right, Kabir says saving is clutching, so spend it now and trust.
he means keep it hidden where nobody can find it, like the knot.
games.why: Kabir turns down both the knot and the sale for one kind of wealth, the Name. he never tells anyone to stop saving.

practice: Find a string, a shoelace, or the corner of a scarf, and tie a firm knot in it. Hold it, feel how tight it is. Then slowly untie it, lay it down, and sit for the rest of the time with your hand open on your knee.
If you'd like, read ang 1158 before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1157. Where Kabir's Bhairao hymns begin, and the weaver calls the Name a wealth he won't knot up or sell.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gaanth, a knot. Kabir says he won't tie the Name's wealth in one.

carryVoice: Kabir: a weaver who left the knot untied. Some wealth you can only keep by not clutching it. That's today.
